title: Mangroves: Nature's Best Tree?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore mangroves, the salt-tolerant trees that grow between land and sea. They cover the term mangrove versus mangal, the red, black and white species and how they zone from shoreline inland, salt-handling methods (secreting in black mangroves, filtering via reverse osmosis-like roots in red mangroves), oxygen-breathing pneumatophores and prop roots, viviparous seedlings that plant themselves, mangrove forests as fish and wildlife nurseries (including Bengal tigers in the Sundarbans and pygmy three-toed sloths in Panama), coastal protection from waves and storm surge (including the 1991 Bangladesh cyclone and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami), carbon sequestration as blue carbon, deforestation drivers such as shrimp farming and invasive species, and restoration and blue bonds. The episode ends with a listener mail from a Satanist listener named Donna and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to mangroves
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce mangroves as a favorite tree, inspired by Josh's trip to Mexico. They note there are roughly 80 to 90 species not all genetically related, where mangroves grow, the size of mangrove forests, the Sundarbans, and where they occur in the United States.

segments.title: Mangrove types and zonation
segments.summary: They describe red mangroves with prop roots along the water's edge, black mangroves with pneumatophores growing slightly further inland, and white mangroves growing furthest inland with normal shallow roots. They explain the zonation from shore inland and the term mangal for a mangrove forest.

segments.title: How mangroves handle salt
segments.summary: Mangroves can grow in salinity up to about 75 parts per thousand. Black mangroves secrete salt onto their leaves, while red mangroves filter salt out at their roots using a reverse-osmosis-like process aided by suberin.

segments.title: Breathing through roots and pneumatophores
segments.summary: Waterlogged, compacted mangrove soil lacks oxygen, so black mangroves use pneumatophores as snorkels and red mangroves use prop roots, both with lenticels for oxygen exchange. The hosts compare this to the root systems of terrestrial trees.

segments.title: Viviparous seedlings and wildlife habitat
segments.summary: Some mangroves are viviparous, producing seedlings on the parent tree that drop and can plant themselves, sprout roots quickly, and float for up to a year. The dense mangal also serves as a nursery for fish, including goliath grouper, and habitat for monkeys, birds, and insects.

segments.title: Bengal tigers and pygmy three-toed sloths
segments.summary: The hosts note the Sundarbans hold the largest single population of Bengal tigers, about a hundred of them. They also say the pygmy three-toed sloth in Panama lives only in mangrove forests.

segments.title: Coastal protection and storm surge
segments.summary: Mangroves reduce wave energy and storm surge, reducing erosion and inland flooding. The hosts cite the 1991 Bangladesh cyclone after mangrove loss and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami study finding mangroves reduced wave heights.

segments.title: Blue carbon, deforestation, shrimp farming, and restoration
segments.summary: Mangroves store carbon in peat and are described as far more efficient at carbon storage than terrestrial vegetation, with about 6.4 billion tons held. Losses from deforestation, especially shrimp farming, and invasive nilgai antelope in Texas are discussed. The hosts note deforestation is slowing, mention restoration, and describe blue bonds.

segments.title: Listener mail from Donna, a Satanist
segments.summary: A listener named Donna, a Satanist, thanks the show for its episode on Satanism and says it helped people understand the practice. The hosts respond to feedback about an opening remark in that episode.
